questions.topic: Focus of a parabola written in vertex form
questions.learningObjective: read the focus of a vertical parabola from its equation
questions.stem: The curve y = 2x^2 has its vertex at the origin and opens upwards along the y-axis. What is the y-coordinate of its focus? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A parabola in the form y = a x squared has focal length p given by 4p = 1 over a, because the standard form y = x squared over 4p must match coefficient for coefficient. With a = 2 that gives 4p = 1 over 2, so p = 1 over 8, and the focus lies a distance p from the vertex along the axis of symmetry, which here is the positive y-direction. The directrix is the mirror image on the other side, at y = minus 1 over 8. The defining property confirms it. Take the point (2, 8) on the curve: its distance to the focus (0, 0.125) is the square root of 4 + 62.015625, that is the square root of 66.015625, which is 8.125, and its distance to the directrix y = -0.125 is 8 + 0.125, again 8.125. Repeating at x = 3, y = 18, both distances come to 18.125, so the focal data is right.
questions.hint: Match the coefficient against the standard form y = x^2 over 4p.

options.text: The coefficient 2 is not p; since 4p = 1 over 2, p = 1 over 8 and the latus rectum is 4p = 0.5
The chord is four times the focal length, so the answer is 8 and the method is already right
options.misconception: takes the leading coefficient of the curve for the focal length, which is a different quantity entirely

options.text: The coefficient must be halved before quadrupling, so the answer is 4 and the arithmetic is sound
options.misconception: applies the right formula to a quantity that was never the focal length in the first place

questions.topic: Eccentricity as the single test for conic type
questions.learningObjective: classify a conic from the value of its eccentricity
questions.stem: A conic is defined as the locus of points for which the distance to a focus is a fixed multiple of the distance to a corresponding directrix. How does the value of that multiple distinguish the three conics?

options.text: A multiple of 0 gives an ellipse, 1 gives a parabola, and 2 gives a hyperbola
options.misconception: believes the ellipse case needs a multiple of zero, confusing a shrinking ratio with a vanishing one

options.text: A multiple below 1 gives a hyperbola, equal to 1 gives a parabola, and above 1 gives an ellipse
options.misconception: reverses the two bounded and unbounded cases, so the ellipse and the hyperbola trade places

options.text: The multiple says nothing about the type, since every conic uses a different focus and directrix
options.misconception: believes the ratio varies from conic to conic without noticing it is the classification itself

options.text: A multiple below 1 gives an ellipse, equal to 1 gives a parabola, and above 1 gives a hyperbola

questions.explanation: The multiple is called the eccentricity, written e, and it is the cleanest classification there is. When e is below 1 the distance to the focus never catches up with the distance to the directrix, the locus closes up, and you get an ellipse; a circle is the limiting case e = 0, where the two foci merge at the centre. When e is exactly 1 the two distances grow at the same rate and the locus runs away without closing, giving a parabola. When e exceeds 1 the focus eventually wins, so the locus splits into two separate branches, which is a hyperbola. The same statement covers the three cases for the reader who prefers ratios: for the ellipse x squared over 25 plus y squared over 16 equal to 1, c is the square root of 25 minus 16, that is 3, and e = 3 over 5, that is 0.6.
questions.hint: Ask whether the focus can ever overtake the directrix as you move away.

A ray travelling parallel to the axis, that is straight down the y-axis, strikes the dish at the point (3, 2.25). Describe where it goes after reflecting, and state the tangent there.

It reflects back along the y-axis, because a curve that is symmetric about the y-axis must send rays back along it
options.misconception: believes symmetry alone fixes the outgoing direction, ignoring the angle-bisecting property of the tangent

options.text: It travels towards the directrix, because the reflected ray always points away from the focus
options.misconception: sends the ray to the directrix, which is where the incoming rays would have come from, not where they go

options.text: It travels along the tangent, since a ray striking a smooth curve always leaves along the tangent
options.misconception: claims the ray leaves along the tangent rather than being reflected by it, which is not how reflection works

questions.explanation: The tangent to y = x squared over 4 has slope x over 2, which at x = 3 is 1.5, and it passes through (3, 2.25), so the tangent is y = 1.5x - 2.25. Substituting that into x squared equal to 4y gives x squared - 6x + 9, that is (x - 3) squared, which has a double root at x = 3, confirming tangency. The reflection can then be computed rather than assumed. The incoming direction is (0, -1), the unit tangent is (1, 1.5) over its length, and reflecting the incoming direction in that line gives (minus 0.9231, minus 0.3846). The unit direction from (3, 2.25) to the focus (0, 1) is exactly (minus 0.9231, minus 0.3846), since the distance is 3.25. So the ray does pass through the focus, and that is exactly why a dish of this shape is a collector rather than a mirror.
questions.hint: Compute the tangent, then reflect the incoming direction in it and compare with the direction to the focus.

questions.topic: Area of a parabolic segment
questions.learningObjective: find the area between a parabola and a line cutting off a segment
questions.stem: The parabola y = 2x^2 is cut by the horizontal line y = 8, which meets it at the points (2, 8) and (-2, 8). What is the area of the region between the line and the parabola, in square units, to four decimal places? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Archimedes found that a parabolic segment has two thirds of the area of the parallelogram on the same base and same height, or equivalently four thirds of the inscribed triangle. Here the inscribed triangle has vertices (0, 0), (2, 8) and (-2, 8), so its base is 4 and its height is 8 and its area is 16, and four thirds of that is 64 over 3, which is 21.3333. An independent numerical integration confirms it without using Archimedes' result at all. Integrating the difference 8 - 2x squared from minus 2 to 2 gives 32 - 16 over 3, that is the square-root-free value 64 over 3, and a trapezoid rule on four million subintervals returns 21.3333 to six decimal places. The two routes agree, which is the point: a closed form inherited from antiquity and a brute-force accumulation should land on the same digits.
questions.hint: The segment is four thirds of the triangle with the same base and vertex.

questions.stem: The ellipse x^2/25 + y^2/16 = 1 has semi-axes a = 5 and b = 4. What is its eccentricity, the ratio of the distance from the centre to a focus over the semi-major axis? Give the answer to three decimal places.

The two routes to c agree. Reading it off the equation gives the square root of 25 minus 16 directly, and measuring it from the two foci and the vertex gives the same, since the point (5, 0) is 2 from one focus and 8 from the other.
questions.hint: c squared is a squared minus b squared for an ellipse, and e is c over a.

questions.topic: Reflection property of an ellipse
questions.learningObjective: state and justify the reflection property of an ellipse
questions.stem: Why does a light ray leaving one focus of an elliptical mirror always arrive at the other focus?

options.misconception: invokes symmetry of the figure, which cannot determine where an individual reflected ray goes

options.text: Because the sum of the two distances is fixed, a reflection that lengthens one leg must shorten the other, and only the minimum path does that
Because the two foci are mirror images of each other across the minor axis of the ellipse

questions.stem: A general second-degree equation Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 has to be reduced to a standard form before its foci or asymptotes can be read off. Put these four steps in the order in which they must occur.

options.text: Scale the remaining equation so the squared terms have denominators 1, and then read off the axes, the foci and the asymptotes
Decide whether the quadratic part has one sign or the other, that is whether B squared - 4AC is negative, zero or positive
If B is not zero, rotate the axes through the angle with cot 2 theta equal to A minus C over B, which removes the cross term
Translate the origin to the centre of the resulting curve, by solving the two linear equations for x and y

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each step needs from the previous one. Deciding the type comes first because B squared minus 4AC is computable straight from the coefficients and it says whether to expect a closed curve, a single branch or two, and it also warns that a zero discriminant may mean a degenerate pair of lines rather than a parabola. Rotation comes next because the cross term has to be gone before the linear terms can be made to vanish, and a translation does not remove a cross term. Translation comes third: once the axes are principal, the curve is symmetric about a point or about a line, and the linear terms locate that point or that line, so solving the two linear equations gives the centre or the vertex. Scaling is last and is purely a matter of rewriting, with the caveat that a general second-degree equation has only five effective coefficients, so a fifth point pins it down and any sixth is redundant. Skipping a step usually means carrying an unnoticed cross term into what looks like a standard form.
questions.hint: Each step needs the previous one to have removed the terms it handles.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why a parabola collects parallel rays
questions.learningObjective: explain the reflection property of a parabola
questions.stem: Explain why a parabolic dish gathers rays travelling parallel to its axis and sends them all through the focus, and check the claim on the parabola y = x squared over 4 with focus at (0, 1).

answer.exemplar: The mechanism is the fixed-distance idea that drives the rest of conic geometry, run in reverse. A point P on a parabola is equidistant from its focus F and from its directrix, so the segment from P to F has exactly the same length as the perpendicular from P down to the directrix. That perpendicular lies along the direction in which an incoming ray parallel to the axis is travelling, so the incoming ray, that perpendicular, and the line to the focus are the two equal legs of an isosceles triangle with vertex P. In an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal, so the ray and the focal line make equal angles with the directrix's perpendicular, which says exactly that the tangent at P bisects the angle between them. By the law of reflection a ray meeting a mirror at normal incidence leaves at the same angle on the other side of the normal, and since the tangent bisects that angle the reflected ray travels along the line to the focus. The numerical check on y = x squared over 4 uses the point (3, 2.25), whose tangent has slope 1.5. Reflecting the incoming direction (0, -1) in that tangent line gives the unit direction (minus 0.9231, minus 0.3846), and the direction from (3, 2.25) to the focus (0, 1) is the vector (minus 3, minus 1.25) divided by its length 3.25, which is the same pair of numbers, so the ray does arrive at the focus. The converse holds as well, a ray from the focus reflecting parallel to the axis, so a dish both collects and re-emits. The mirror-image behaviour of an ellipse is the contrast case, and it is the only other conic that reflects rays, which is why elliptical and parabolic reflectors rather than hyperbolic ones are the ones built.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: One definition covering every conic
questions.learningObjective: prove that a single focus-directrix definition yields all the conics
questions.stem: Prove that the locus of points whose distance from a fixed focus is a fixed multiple e of the distance from a fixed directrix is an ellipse when e is below 1, a parabola when e is 1 and a hyperbola when e is above 1.

answer.exemplar: Fix a focus F and a directrix, which is a line at perpendicular distance d from F, and let e be the positive constant of the ratio. Choose coordinates with the directrix on the line x = minus d and the focus at the origin, so F = (0, 0) and the distance from F to the directrix is d. A point P = (x, y) on the locus satisfies the square root of x squared plus y squared equal to e times the distance from P to the line x = minus d, which is x + d provided x is to the right of the directrix, as it must be for any point of the locus. Squaring gives x squared plus y squared equal to e squared times the quantity x + d squared, that is x squared plus y squared = e squared x squared + 2 e squared d x + e squared d squared. Case one, e less than 1. Move everything to the left and complete the square in x. The equation becomes one half, x + e squared d over one minus e squared, squared, plus y squared, equal to e squared d squared over one minus e squared. Both coefficients on the left are positive, so this is an ellipse, with its centre on the x-axis and its two foci at the origin and its mirror image, and the focal distance from the centre is the absolute value of e squared d over one minus e squared. Case two, e equal to 1. The x squared terms cancel, leaving y squared = 2 d x plus d squared, or y squared = 2 d times the quantity x plus d over 2, which is a parabola with focus at the origin and vertex at minus d over 2, in agreement with the standard form. Case three, e greater than 1. Now the two x squared terms have opposite signs, so completing the square gives an equation with a minus sign on one axis, which is a hyperbola with two branches, its foci again on the x-axis. In every case the eccentricity of the resulting conic works out to be exactly e, so the parameter in the definition and the eccentricity of the curve are the same number. The proof is complete.

questions.explanation: The proof works by squaring the definition and completing the square, and the sign of the surviving quadratic coefficient is what separates the three cases. The two cases differ only in the sign of one minus e squared, so a single computation covers both. The algebraic trap to avoid is completing the square before moving the linear terms to the other side, since the halves that get put back then come out with the wrong sign; the direct substitution of the centre, where the original left-hand side must equal minus the radius squared, is the check that catches it.
questions.hint: Put the directrix on x = -d and the focus at the origin, then square and complete the square.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why a ratio of distances traces a circle
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fixed distance ratio gives a circle rather than another conic
questions.stem: Explain why the set of points at a fixed ratio of distances from two fixed points is a circle, and derive its centre and radius in the case where the ratio is 2 and the two fixed points are 6 units apart on a line.

answer.exemplar: The reason is that squaring the ratio condition produces equal coefficients on x squared and y squared, and that is precisely the signature of a circle. Take the fixed points at A = (0, 0) and B = (6, 0), and let the ratio of the distance to A over the distance to B be k. The condition is the square root of x squared plus y squared equal to k times the square root of the quantity x - 6 squared plus y squared. Squaring once removes the two roots and gives x squared plus y squared = k squared times the quantity x squared - 12x + 36 + y squared. Collecting, one minus k squared times the quantity x squared plus y squared, plus 12 k squared x, minus 36 k squared, all equal to 0. Dividing through by one minus k squared, when that is not zero, gives x squared plus y squared, plus 12 k squared over one minus k squared times x, minus 36 k squared over one minus k squared, equal to 0, and the two squared terms carry the same coefficient, which no other conic can do except a circle. With k = 2 the coefficient is one minus 4, that is minus 3, and the equation becomes 3x squared plus 3y squared - 48x plus 144 equal to 0; dividing by 3 gives x squared plus y squared - 16x plus 48 equal to 0, and completing the square gives the quantity x - 8 squared plus y squared equal to 16, a circle of radius 4 centred at (8, 0). The centre sits beyond B rather than between A and B because k exceeds 1. In general, for two points a distance d apart and a ratio k not equal to 1, the radius is d k over the absolute value of k squared minus 1, and the centre lies on the line through A and B at distance d k squared over k squared minus 1 from A. The case k equal to 1 is the exception, since then the equation degenerates to the single straight line through A and B perpendicular to their joining line, which is the locus of points equidistant from the two.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Asymptote read off with a stale constant
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a wrong asymptote and confirm the correction by a crossing test
questions.stem: The hyperbola x^2/9 - y^2/16 = 1 has a pair of asymptotes through the origin. A student reports them as y = 3x/4 and y = -3x/4, reasoning that the slope is the ratio of the two denominators, and is confident because those lines do pass through the centre. What is the error, and what test settles it?

options.text: The slope should be b squared over a, that is 16 over 3, so neither of the student's lines is right
options.misconception: squares the semi-conjugate axis into the numerator, which over-steepens the lines

options.text: The slope is the ratio of the semi-axes, 4 over 3, and the reversed lines really do cross the curve at x = 48 over the square root of 175
The slope is correct, and the fact that the lines pass through the centre is all an asymptote has to satisfy
options.misconception: believes passing through the centre is the whole test for an asymptote, ignoring the no-crossing requirement

options.text: The asymptotes of a hyperbola through the origin are always the coordinate axes, whatever the denominators are
options.misconception: borrows the asymptotes of xy = 6 and applies them to an axis-aligned hyperbola

questions.explanation: The slope of an asymptote of x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared is b over a, which here is 4 over 3, not 3 over 4. The student has inverted the ratio of the denominators. The decisive test is not whether the line passes through the centre, since the wrong lines do, but whether the line ever meets the curve, because an asymptote approaches without touching. Substitute y = 4x over 3: the equation becomes x squared over 9 minus 16x squared over 9 over 16, and 16 over 16 cancels, leaving x squared over 9 minus x squared over 9, which is 0 for every x, so the equation collapses to 0 = 1 and the line never meets the curve. Now substitute the student's y = 3x over 4: the equation becomes x squared over 9 minus 9x squared over 16 over 16, that is x squared times 0.111111 minus 0.035156, which equals 1, giving a genuine crossing at x = 3.6285, that is 48 over the square root of 175. So the reversed lines are secants of the hyperbola, not asymptotes of it.
questions.hint: An asymptote must never meet the curve, so substitute the candidate slope and look for a solution.

questions.topic: Power of a point with the subtraction reversed
questions.learningObjective: correct a power-of-a-point computation in which the subtraction runs the wrong way
questions.stem: The point (13, 0) lies outside the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25. A student computes the power as the radius squared minus the distance squared, that is 25 - 169, and reports minus 144, then concludes the point must be inside the circle. What is wrong, and what is the power?

options.text: The power is correctly minus 144, since a point outside a circle always has a negative power
options.misconception: accepts the reversed subtraction and the wrong interpretation at the same time

options.text: The power is 26, the sum of the radius and the distance, which is what a secant segment pair adds to
options.misconception: adds the two lengths instead of subtracting their squares, mixing up a sum with a difference

options.text: The subtraction runs the other way, so the power is 169 - 25, that is 144, which is positive outside the circle
The subtraction runs the other way and the power is 144, but a positive power means the point is inside
options.misconception: gets the sign of the power right and then inverts what the sign means about inside or outside

questions.explanation: The power of a point is the distance from the point to the centre squared, minus the radius squared, and the order matters because the sign carries the geometry: a point outside gives a positive power, a point on the circle gives zero, and a point inside gives a negative one. With the distance 13 and the radius 5 the power is 169 - 25, that is 144, and the point is indeed outside, since 13 is greater than 5. Three checks confirm 144. The distance from (13, 0) to the centre is 13 and the radius is 5, so the tangent length is the square root of 144, that is 12, and 5, 12 and 13 form a right triangle. A secant along the x-axis cuts the circle at (5, 0) and (-5, 0), which are 8 and 18 units from the point, and 8 times 18 is 144. And the reversed order gives minus 144, the sign that belongs to an interior point, which is the whole reason the error is easy to make and easy to catch.
questions.hint: Decide which quantity is larger, because the subtraction must start with the larger one.

questions.topic: Centre and radius of a circle with a stale constant
questions.learningObjective: complete the square for a circle and notice a dropped constant
questions.stem: The circle x^2 + y^2 - 18x + 2y - 27 = 0 is to be put in centre-radius form. A student moves the constant to the other side, completes the square, and gets the quantity x - 9 squared plus the quantity y + 1 squared equal to 82, reporting a radius of about 9.06. What was left out?

options.text: The 18 should be halved before it is squared, so the radius squared is 9 plus 1 plus 27, that is 37
options.misconception: halves the linear coefficient instead of squaring it, treating the two steps as the same operation

options.text: The 27 should be subtracted, so the radius squared is 81 + 1 - 27, that is 55, and the radius is about 7.42
options.misconception: keeps the constant on the wrong side of the equation when completing the square

options.text: Nothing was left out, because completing the square never uses the constant term
options.misconception: believes the constant drops out of a centre-radius calculation, which it emphatically does not

options.text: The 27 has to be added, so the radius squared is 81 + 1 + 27, that is 109, and the radius is about 10.44

questions.explanation: Completing the square uses the constant, because the half of the squared linear term has to be put back. Writing x squared minus 18x as the quantity x - 9 squared minus 81, and y squared plus 2y as the quantity y + 1 squared minus 1, the equation becomes the quantity x - 9 squared plus the quantity y + 1 squared, minus 81 minus 1 minus 27, equal to 0. So the squares equal 81 + 1 + 27, that is 109, and the radius is the square root of 109, which is 10.4403. The student's 82 is 81 + 1 with the 27 left behind, and that omission moves the radius by more than a unit. A direct test settles which is right: put the centre (9, -1) into the original left-hand side, giving 81 + 1 - 162 + 2 - 27, which is minus 109, and the left-hand side of a centre-radius equation at the centre must be minus the radius squared, so the radius squared is 109. The centre is unaffected either way, which is exactly why the error survives a quick glance.

questions.topic: How often a line can meet a hyperbola
questions.learningObjective: bound the number of intersections between a line and a hyperbola
questions.stem: A straight line is drawn across the hyperbola x^2/9 - y^2/16 = 1. What is the largest number of points at which the two can meet?

options.text: Two, because substituting a line for y leaves a quadratic in x, and a quadratic has at most two roots
One, because a hyperbola has two branches and each branch can be met at most once
options.misconception: counts branches rather than roots, and would also rule out the two crossings a line makes on one branch

options.text: Four, because each of the two branches can be met twice over
options.misconception: doubles the bound by counting each branch twice, which a quadratic cannot do

options.text: No fixed bound, because a line can run along a branch and meet it at every point
options.misconception: confuses a secant with an asymptote, which approaches a branch without ever lying on it

questions.explanation: The bound comes from the degree of the equation, and it is exactly two. Write the line as y = m x plus c and substitute into x squared over 9 minus y squared over 16 equal to 1. The result is a quadratic in x, and a quadratic has at most two real roots unless it vanishes identically, which would require the line to lie on the curve, and no line does because the hyperbola is not a union of lines. Both roots can be real: the line y = 0 gives x squared over 9 = 1, so x = 3 and x = -3, two crossings, one on each branch. A tangent is the boundary case, where the two roots coincide into a double root, as with the tangent at (3, 0) whose line is x = 3. And when the quadratic has no real root the line misses the curve altogether, which is the fate of the asymptotes.
questions.hint: Substitute the line into the conic and count the degree of what is left.

questions.topic: Which of a and b is the semi-major axis
questions.learningObjective: identify the semi-major axis in a standard-form ellipse
questions.stem: The ellipse is written as x^2/25 + y^2/4 = 1. Which pair of statements about its axes is correct?

options.text: Both semi-axes are 2, because the smaller denominator is the one that counts
options.misconception: reads only the second denominator, so the shape again comes out as a circle of radius 2

options.text: The semi-major axis is 5 along the x-axis and the semi-minor axis is 2 along the y-axis
The semi-major axis is 2 along the y-axis and the semi-minor axis is 5 along the x-axis
options.misconception: assigns the larger length to the y-axis merely because y is written second in the equation

options.text: Both semi-axes are 5, because the first denominator is the one that counts
options.misconception: reads only the first denominator, so the shape comes out as a circle of radius 5

questions.explanation: The major axis is the longer one, so the rule is simply to compare the two denominators after taking their square roots, and to attach each to the axis it belongs to. Here the square roots are 5 for the x term and 2 for the y term, so the major axis is 5 along x and the minor is 2 along y. The names are worth pinning down, because a shorter axis is not a worse one: the major axis is the one the foci sit on, and those foci are at the square root of 25 - 4, that is the square root of 21, which is 4.5826 from the centre along the x-axis. Two of the distances here are equal, since 4 and 4 add to 8. The eccentricity is then 4.5826 over 5, that is 0.9165, and because it is close to 1 the ellipse is a long thin shape, which is consistent with a minor semi-axis of only 2.
questions.hint: Take the square root of each denominator and keep track of which axis it belongs to.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why the conics are named after the cutting plane
questions.learningObjective: explain the naming of the conic sections by the angle of the cutting plane
questions.stem: A plane cutting a cone at right angles to its axis gives a circle, and a plane cutting it parallel to one generator gives a parabola. Why does the angle of the plane decide the shape, and what happens in between?

options.text: The names record how the plane was moved, and two cones of different sizes can give the same curve
options.misconception: treats the name as a record of the motion rather than of the resulting shape

options.text: The names are historical accidents with no geometric content behind them
options.misconception: dismisses the terminology as arbitrary, when in fact each name describes the cut that produces it

options.text: Tilting the plane lets the curve close up or split in two, and at the parallel setting it just fails to close, so the name records the cut
The names record the number of axes each curve has, since a circle has none and a parabola has one
options.misconception: attributes the naming to the axis count, which is a consequence of the cut rather than its cause

questions.explanation: A cone is a surface of revolution, so every cross-section of one is a scaled and possibly sheared version of a single family of curves, and the angle of the cut selects a member of that family. A plane at right angles to the axis meets every generator at the same distance from the vertex, and the set of points at a fixed distance from the vertex in that plane is a circle, which is why that cut is called a circle. A plane parallel to one generator meets that generator at no finite point, so the curve never closes and runs out to infinity in one direction: a parabola. Any tilt between the two splits the difference, closing the curve into an ellipse when the tilt is less than a right angle and opening it into two branches, a hyperbola, when the tilt is greater. The eccentricity tracks the tilt continuously, from 0 for the perpendicular cut through 1 at the parallel cut to values above 1 beyond it, so the naming and the parameter are two readings of the same geometric fact.
questions.hint: Ask whether the curve can close up at all for the given tilt.

questions.topic: Locating a focus and then measuring from it
questions.learningObjective: combine finding a parabola's focus with measuring a focal distance
questions.stem: For the parabola y = x^2 the focus lies on the y-axis a distance p above the vertex, with 4p equal to 1. First, state the coordinates of the focus. Second, state the distance from that focus to the point (4, 16) on the curve. Select every statement that is correct.

options.text: Second: the distance is 16.25, because the offsets from (0, 0.25) to (4, 16) are 4 and 15.75
Second: the distance is 16.25, confirmed because the directrix y = -0.25 is 16.25 from the point as well
options.misconception: checks the answer against the other half of the definition, which is the only way to be sure the figure is right

options.text: First: the focus is at (0, 4), because the focus is always the square root of the coefficient of x squared
options.misconception: puts the focus four units up, having read the point (4, 16) as though it were the focal parameter

options.text: First: the focus is at (0, 0.25), because 4p = 1 gives p = 0.25 and the focus is p above the vertex

The standard form is y = x squared over 4p, and the leading coefficient here is 1, so 4p = 1 and p = 0.25, and since the vertex is the origin and the curve opens upwards the focus is at (0, 0.25). Stage two measures from there. The point (4, 16) is on the curve because 16 is the square of 4, and the vector from the focus to that point is (4, 15.75), whose length is the square root of 16 + 248.0625, that is the square root of 264.0625, and 264.0625 is 4225 over 16, so the distance is 65 over 4, that is 16.25. The third statement confirms it by the other half of the definition: the directrix is y = -0.25, and the distance from (4, 16) to that line is 16 + 0.25, again 16.25, and the agreement of the two distances is exactly what certifies that the point is on the parabola built from that focus and directrix. The fourth statement fails because 0.25 comes from dividing 1 by 4, not from any square root.
